parsed.gloss: hazāroñ = thousands; ḳhvāhisheñ = desires, wishes; aisī = such; ki = that; har = every; ḳhvāhish = desire, wish; pe = upon; dam = breath, life; nikle = comes out, departs; bahut = many, much; nikle = came out, were fulfilled; mire = my; armān = longings, unfulfilled desires; lekin = but; phir bhī = even then, still; kam = few, less; nikle = came out, were fulfilled
parsed.literal: Thousands of desires are such that at every desire the breath would depart; many of my longings came out, but even then they came out few.
parsed.poetic: Thousands of desires, each worth dying for; many of them I have realized, yet still too few.
notes: dam nikle: literally 'the breath comes out,' an idiom for dying or giving up one's life; here it means each desire is so intense it could kill.

nikle in the second line shifts meaning: the same verb means both 'to come out' of the body as breath and 'to be fulfilled, to emerge into reality' for desires. The repetition is the central wordplay.
armān: in the ghazal tradition this is not just any desire but a longing, often unfulfilled or impossible, carrying a tone of regret.
phir bhī kam nikle: the paradox that even many fulfilled desires feel too few, because desire itself is endless.
The first line sets up hyperbolic scale (thousands of desires, each fatal), the second undercuts it with the melancholy admission that even 'many' is not enough.
parsed.lost: The double sense of nikle as both 'breath departing' and 'desire being fulfilled' cannot be reproduced in English with a single verb. The idiomatic dam nikle, with its physical image of the last breath leaving the body, flattens into 'worth dying for.' The ghazal's stock symbol of armān as a specifically unfulfilled, aching longing is only approximated by 'longings' or 'desires.'

parsed.gloss: na thā kuchh = nothing existed / there was nothing; to = then; ḳhudā thā = God was/existed; kuchh na hotā = if nothing existed / if there were nothing; ḳhudā hotā = God would be/exist; Duboyā = drowned, ruined (causative of ḍūbnā); mujh ko = me; hone ne = by being/existence (verbal noun of honā); na hotā maiñ = if I were not / had I not existed; to kyā hotā = then what would be/have happened
parsed.literal:
When nothing existed, God existed; if nothing existed, God would exist.
Existence drowned me; if I were not, then what would be?
parsed.poetic:
When nothing was, God was; if nothing were, God would be.
Being has drowned me; had I not been, what would be?
notes: The first line contrasts actual past (thā, 'was') with the hypothetical/subjunctive (hotā, 'would be'), making God the one necessary existence before and apart from all contingent things.
kuchh can mean 'anything' or 'something'; I used 'nothing' to keep the paradox that both the absence of creation and the absence of the self point to God.
hone is the verbal noun of honā ('to be/become/happen'); 'Being' in English preserves the philosophical sense of existence as an active force, though it loses the 'becoming/happening' nuance.
Duboyā literally means 'drowned' and idiomatically means 'ruined/undone'; I kept 'drowned' in the poetic version to retain the water/annihilation image.

The final kyā hotā is deliberately open: it can mean 'what would exist?', 'what would happen?', or 'what would I be?'. It echoes khudā hotā from the first line, hinting that without the ego-self only God would remain.
No pen name (takhallus) appears in this particular sher.
parsed.lost: The single verb-root honā repeated as thā/hotā/hone/hotā/hotā, which knits existence, becoming, and happening together; the exact subjunctive/conditional resonance of hotā; the ambiguity of kuchh and kyā; and the Sufi implication of drowning as ego-annihilation are only partly carried by 'Being' and 'what would be?'.

parsed.literal:
O naive heart, what has happened to you?

notes: dil-e-nādāñ is a vocative with Persian izāfat; I render it as 'O naive heart' to keep the direct address.
nādāñ carries both 'ignorant/innocent' and 'foolish'; the heart is gently reproached for falling into love without knowing its cost. 'Naive' keeps the innocence but softens the affectionate scolding.
āḳhir can mean 'after all', 'in the end', or 'ultimately'; it makes the second line a rhetorical question. I use 'After all' to preserve that exasperated turn.

dard and davā form a medical metaphor: pain and remedy. In ghazal convention, love's pain is often incurable, or its only cure is the beloved, who remains inaccessible. English 'pain' and 'cure' keep the metaphor but not the full Sufi/love register.
The couplet is a self-address to the heart, splitting the speaker from his own feeling; I keep that direct second-person address.

notes: 'Ghalib' is the poet's pen name (takhallus) and also means 'victor/dominant'; the line ironically turns the 'victor' into someone useless.
nikammā and kaam ke share the root kaam (work/use): nikammā means without work or useless, while kaam ke means of use or capable.
The phrase 'aadmī kaam ke' is an idiom for a capable or useful man; I rendered it as 'man of use' to keep its plain, colloquial force.
The grammar makes love the active agent: ishq ne ... kar diyā, love is what has ruined him.
The pronoun 'ham' can be plural, royal, or a modest singular; in the poetic version I used 'I' because the ghazal speaker is Ghalib himself.

parsed.gloss: ham ko = to us; ma.alūm hai = is known; jannat = paradise/heaven; kī = of; haqīqat = reality/truth/essence; lekin = but; dil ke = of the heart; ḳhush rakhne ko = to keep happy/pleased; 'ġhālib' = pen name of the poet; ye = this; ḳhayāl = thought/idea/fancy; achchhā hai = is good
parsed.literal:
To us is known the reality of paradise, but
To keep the heart happy, Ghalib, this fancy is good.
parsed.poetic:
We know full well the truth of paradise, and yet,
To keep the heart content, Ghalib, this dream is sweet.
notes: The pen name 'Ghalib' appears in the second line as a self-address, a standard ghazal convention where the poet speaks to himself in the final couplet.
'ḳhayāl' carries the double sense of 'thought/idea' and 'fancy/illusion' — the poet knowingly calls the concept of paradise a pleasing illusion rather than a literal truth.
The couplet enacts a tension between intellectual honesty (knowing paradise's 'reality') and emotional need (keeping the heart happy), a hallmark of Ghalib's philosophical skepticism.
'dil ke ḳhush rakhne ko' is an idiom meaning 'to console oneself' or 'to keep oneself content' — I rendered it as 'to keep the heart content' to preserve the idiomatic flavor.

The word 'haqīqat' in Sufi vocabulary means ultimate reality or essence, not just factual truth — this adds a mystical layer: the speaker may know paradise's true spiritual essence, yet still treats the popular conception as a consoling fancy.

parsed.gloss: reḳhte ke = of Rekhta (the old name for Urdu/Hindi poetry, esp. the mixed language); tumhīñ = you alone/only you; ustād = master, expert; nahīñ ho = are not; ġhālib = pen name, lit. 'dominant, victorious'; kahte haiñ = they say; agle zamāne meñ = in an earlier age/time; koī = someone, a certain; mīr = Mir (Taqi Mir), also lit. 'leader, chief'; bhī thā = also was
parsed.literal:
You alone are not the master of Rekhta, Ghalib —
They say in an earlier age there was also a certain Mir.
parsed.poetic:
You are not the only master of Rekhta, Ghalib —
They say in ages past there was also one Mir.
notes: The addressee is Ghalib himself, addressed by his pen name (takhallus) in the second person — a classic ghazal signature move, here turned into self-irony.

'Rekhta' is the older term for Urdu, literally 'poured/mixed', referring to the blended Persian-Arabic-Indic poetic language. I keep the term untranslated in the poetic version to preserve its historical weight.
'Ghalib' means 'dominant/victorious', so the line plays on the pen name: the one called 'Dominant' is told he is not the sole master.
'Mir' is both the name of Mir Taqi Mir, the great predecessor poet, and a common noun meaning 'leader/chief'. The indefinite 'koī mīr' (a certain Mir / some Mir) lets both readings hover.
The tone is gently deflating, almost conversational — 'they say' (kahte haiñ) frames the claim as received wisdom, not the speaker's own judgment.
parsed.lost: The full resonance of 'Rekhta' as a term for the mixed language itself is hard to carry; English readers may not feel the historical rivalry between Ghalib and Mir, or the double sense of 'Mir' as name and title. The self-address by pen name, with its built-in irony ('Ghalib' = dominant), also loses its immediate force in translation.

parsed.gloss: bas-ki: so much that / to such an extent; dushvār: difficult; har kaam: every task, every affair; āsāñ honā: becoming easy; aadmī: man (mere mortal, descendant of Adam); bhī: even; mayassar nahīñ: is not attainable/available; insāñ honā: to become truly human/humane.
parsed.literal:
So difficult is the becoming-easy of every task
that even for man, becoming human is not attainable.
parsed.poetic:
So hard it is for any task to turn easy,
that even a mere man cannot manage to become truly human.
notes: The first line is a paradox: ease itself (āsāñ honā) is called difficult (dushvār). I kept the paradox in both literal and poetic versions.

The key wordplay is aadmī versus insāñ. Both can mean 'man/human', but aadmī suggests the natural, mortal descendant of Adam, while insāñ implies ethical, fully realized humanity. I used 'mere man' and 'truly human' to mark the distinction.
bas-ki is a Persian conjunction meaning 'so much that/to such an extent'; the English 'so... that...' construction carries the logical consequence.
mayassar means not just 'possible' but 'made available/attainable', often with a nuance of opportunity or grace. 'Attainable' captures part of this, but not the full sense of being granted.
parsed.lost: The sharp aadmī/insāñ distinction is flattened in English, since both can be 'man' or 'human'. The nuance of mayassar as something divinely or circumstantially made available is weakened. The compact Persian-Urdu noun phrases, rhyme, and metre cannot be carried over.

parsed.gloss: pattā pattā = every single leaf; buuTā buuTā = every single plant; haal hamārā = our condition/state; jaane hai = knows; jaane na jaane = whether or not (he/she/it) knows; gul = the rose (also the beloved); hī = only/just; baaġh = garden; to = indeed/but; saarā = the whole/entire
parsed.literal:
Every leaf, every plant knows our condition;
Whether or not (the beloved) knows, even if the rose alone does not know, the whole garden indeed knows.
parsed.poetic:
Each leaf, each sprig, each bough can tell the state I'm in;
The rose may not — but all the garden knows the state I'm in.
notes: The repetition 'pattā pattā buuTā buuTā' (every leaf, every plant) is an idiomatic intensifier meaning 'absolutely everything in nature' — I rendered it with a triple parallel structure to echo the incantatory rhythm.
'Gul' (rose) is the stock symbol for the beloved in the ghazal tradition — beautiful, proud, and indifferent to the lover's suffering. The beloved is singled out as the one who may not know.
The contrast between the single rose (the beloved) and the whole garden (the world, all creation) is the central conceit: the entire universe witnesses the lover's pain except the one it is for.

There is a Sufi resonance: the garden as the whole of creation witnessing the lover's longing, while the Divine Beloved remains seemingly heedless — yet the garden's knowledge is itself a sign of the Beloved's presence.
The verb 'jaane hai' is colloquial/idiomatic for 'jaantā hai' (knows), and the ambiguity of 'jaane na jaane' (may know or may not know) is preserved in my rendering.
The final line has a turn (the 'sher' structure): it begins by doubting the beloved's knowledge, then lands on the certainty that the whole garden knows — I kept this turn intact.
parsed.lost: The sonic texture of the repeated 'pattā pattā buuTā buuTā' with its alliterative plosives and the internal rhyme of 'jaane' occurring four times in two lines cannot be fully reproduced. The grammatical ambiguity of 'jaane' (third-person singular subjunctive 'may know' versus colloquial present 'knows') is flattened in English. The stock ghazal symbolism of 'gul' as the beloved carries centuries of Persian-Urdu poetic resonance that 'rose' only partially conveys. The colloquial register of 'jaane hai' (versus formal 'jaantā hai') gives the original an intimate, folk-wisdom quality that formal English cannot match.

All schemes/remedies were turned upside down; the medicine did nothing.
I saw: this heart-sickness at last finished the work.

The negative kaam kiyā (medicine 'did no work') sets up the second line's kaam tamām kiyā, which means both 'completed the work' and idiomatically 'finished someone off/made an end'.
I used 'finish everything' to echo the finality of kaam tamām kiyā, though the idiom's deathly overtone remains stronger in Urdu.

parsed.literal:
Make the self so high that before every destiny
God Himself asks the servant: tell, what is your will?
parsed.poetic:
Raise the self to such heights that, before each fate is sealed,
God Himself asks His servant: “Tell me, what is your will?”
notes: khudi is Iqbal’s central concept of selfhood or sovereign ego, not mere arrogance; I render it as “the self” or “selfhood.”
There is sound-play among khudi (selfhood), khuda (God), and khud (Himself/self) across the two lines; English cannot reproduce this consonance.
taqdir means fate or divine decree; “before every destiny” implies the perfected self is consulted before God writes each decree.
raza in Islamic idiom usually means the servant’s submission to God’s will; here the relation is inverted—God asks the servant’s raza, a bold theological reversal.
The couplet expresses Iqbal’s idea of the self-actualized human as God’s co-worker, not a passive fatalist.
parsed.lost: The English cannot carry over the khudi/khuda/khud sound-play, nor the full shock of the inversion where God asks the servant’s raza—a word normally associated with human submission to divine will.

parsed.literal:
Iqbal is not despairing of his barren field;
If it becomes slightly moist, then this soil is very fertile, O cupbearer.
parsed.poetic:
Iqbal does not despair of his own barren ground—
Moisten it once, cupbearer, and this soil will abound.
notes: The 'sāqī' (cupbearer) is a central ghazal figure — in Sufi reading, the divine dispenser of grace, wine, or spiritual nourishment. Iqbal addresses the sāqī directly, asking for even a drop of moisture.
'Kisht-e-vīrāñ' (barren field) is a metaphor for the poet's inner state, creative potential, or the Muslim ummah — seemingly desolate but latently fertile.
'Zarḳhez' literally means 'gold-producing' (zar = gold, ḳhez = rising/producing), so the soil is not just fertile but capable of yielding treasure — a wordplay on hidden value.
The pen name 'Iqbāl' (meaning 'prosperity, good fortune') appears in the first line, as required by the ghazal convention of the maqtā (final couplet).
The conditional 'zarā nam ho to' (if it becomes slightly moist) suggests that only a small amount of grace or effort is needed to unlock great potential — a theme of hope against despair.
parsed.lost: The double resonance of 'zarḳhez' as both 'fertile' and 'gold-yielding' cannot be fully carried into English. The name 'Iqbāl' meaning 'prosperity' creates an irony with the 'barren field' that English readers miss. The intimate, almost imperative tone of addressing the sāqī — with its Sufi connotations of the divine beloved or spiritual guide — is flattened in translation. The rhyme and meter of the Urdu ghazal couplet are also inevitably lost.

parsed.literal: If we even sigh, we become defamed; / If they even commit murder, there is no talk.
parsed.poetic: When we so much as sigh, our name is dragged in shame; / When they commit murder, no one even speaks the blame.
notes: Āh (sigh) is a stock ghazal symbol for the lover's suppressed grief and longing — the mildest possible expression of pain, contrasted with qatl (murder), the most extreme act of violence.

Badnām (defamed) vs. charchā na honā (not becoming a topic of talk) sets up an ironic inversion: the powerless cannot even sigh without public scandal, while the powerful can kill and the world remains silent.
The antithesis between 'we' (ham) and 'they' (vo) points to a social or political critique — Allahabadi is known for satirical commentary on colonial-era hypocrisy and double standards.
The repetition of 'bhī... to' (even... then) in both lines creates a parallel structure that sharpens the irony.

In the poetic rendering I used 'dragged in shame' to carry the weight of badnām, and 'no one even speaks the blame' to render the chilling silence of charchā na honā, though it slightly expands the original.
parsed.lost: The extreme economy of the Urdu — the way 'charchā' (gossip/talk) sits as the opposite of 'badnām' (defamed) and implies a society that only notices the powerless — cannot be fully compressed into English. The ghazal's register of āh as a conventional lover's sigh is also culturally specific; in English it reads as simply 'sigh' without the accumulated weight of the ghazal tradition. The passive-impersonal quality of 'charchā nahīñ hotā' (there is no talk) is more chilling in Urdu than any English equivalent.

parsed.literal:
Mir has come, having become an infidel, into God’s house;
on his forehead is a qashqa, around his waist is a zunnar.
parsed.poetic:
Mir has come into God’s house, turned infidel—
a tilak on his forehead, a zunnar around his waist.
notes: The pen name Mīr appears in the first line, marking this as a maqta; it also means ‘leader/chief,’ adding irony: a leader arrives as an infidel.

Qashqa and zunnār are stock symbols of religious otherness—especially Hindu or Christian—and in the ghazal tradition they often signal the lover’s rejection of outward orthodoxy for the religion of love.

ḳhudā ke ghar (‘God’s house’) is literally a mosque or the Kaaba; the image is deliberately scandalous: entering the holy place bearing marks of infidelity. In Sufi idiom it may also suggest the heart as God’s true house.
I kept ‘Mir’ and the foreign markers in the literal version; in the poetic version I used ‘tilak’ for qashqa and kept ‘zunnar’ to preserve the cultural shock.
parsed.lost: The rhyme (ghar/kamar) and meter are lost. The double sense of ‘kāfir ho kar’ as both ‘as an infidel’ and ‘having become an infidel’ cannot be fully captured. The exact sectarian markers qashqa and zunnār have no English equivalent; ‘tilak’ and ‘zunnar’ retain the foreignness but not the full resonance for readers unfamiliar with the tradition. The pen name’s meaning ‘leader’ is also lost if read only as a name.
